Before adjudicating upon the issues framed in the present suit,
it necessary to dwell upon the plethora of pleadings in the present suit.

AVERMENTS OF THE PLAINT: -
3. Succinctly, it is the case of the Plaintiff that She is the absolute owner and in possession of property bearing No. 129A, R- Extension, Mohan Garden, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi-110059 ( herein after referred as to "suit property"), measuring 50 square yards and comprising a ground floor with two rooms, kitchen, latrine, and bathroom, and a first floor with one room.
The plaintiff allowed her son --the defendant--to reside in the suit property as a licensee out of love and affection.
The defendant is married to Smt. Darksha Sheikh and has two children from the said marriage.

4. Further mentioned that however, shortly after the marriage,
the defendant and his wife started misbehaving with the plaintiff, using abusive language, assaulting her, and denying her basic necessities like food and medicine.

Due to continued harassment and threats to her life,
including attempts to involve anti-social elements to forcibly retain the property, the plaintiff, by way of a public notice dated 12.06.2019 published in the newspaper "Virat Vaibhav", debarred the defendant and his family from all her movable and immovable properties and revoked the license granted to him.

5. It is further averred that despite repeated verbal and written requests, including a legal notice dated 28.08.2019 sent via Speed Post,
the defendant refused to vacate the premises and instead threatened the plaintiff with dire consequences.

The defendant has also attempted to sell or create third-party interest in the suit property using false and fabricated documents, which came to the plaintiff's knowledge through reliable Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 2 of 21  sources.

6. Furthermore, on multiple occasions, the plaintiff approached the local police at PS Ranhola to file complaints against the defendant's acts of abuse, harassment, and threats, but no legal action was taken, and she was advised to approach the court.
Consequently, due to fear for her safety, the plaintiff was forced to leave her own house and has been living with her daughter since 25.02.2022.

7. The Plaintiff further submits that she continues to be the lawful and rightful owner of the suit property and maintains constructive possession thereof, as her personal belongings, valuables, and household effects remain within the premises.
The Defendant, who was initially permitted to occupy the suit property as a licensee, is now wrongfully and unlawfully retaining possession, having no legal right, title, or interest therein.

It is further submitted that the Defendant has become an unauthorized occupant and is willfully obstructing the Plaintiff's ingress into the suit property, thereby unlawfully depriving her of access and enjoyment of her own premises.

44. Final arguments advanced by both parties were heard on 08.08.2025.
45.

The file has been carefully and minutely perused and my issue-wise findings with reasons thereof are as under: -
 Issue No.1  Whether the plaintiff is entitled to a decree of permanent and mandatory  injunction, as prayed for? ...OPP.
46.
The burden of proof lies upon the Plaintiff to establish that she is entitled to the relief of permanent and mandatory injunction.
The Plaintiff claims to be the absolute owner of the suit property comprising the ground and first floors and alleges that she was in prior possession.
According to her, the Defendant was permitted to reside in the property as a licensee, along with his wife and children, out of love and affection.

47. Plaintiff further claims that after the Defendant's marriage,
both he and his wife began harassing her and threatened to take over the property.
Due to fear for her safety, the plaintiff was forced to leave her own house and has been living with her daughter since 25.02.2022.

She contends that the license granted to the Defendant was revoked through a public notice dated 12.06.2019 and followed by a legal notice dated 28.08.2019, directing the Defendant to vacate the premises.

Despite this,
the Defendant continued to occupy the suit property.

48. In support of its title and possession claim, Plaintiff has relied upon the copy of Aadhar Card (Ex. PW1/1); Site Plan (Ex. PW1/2);
Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 13 of 21
In response, the Defendant has denied the Plaintiff's ownership and possession of the suit property.

He has asserted that he is the true and lawful owner, having purchased the property in the year 2001 for a consideration of 90,000/-, and has thereafter constructed a building thereon from his own resources.
The Defendant has further alleged that the present suit is collusive in nature and has been instituted at the behest of the Plaintiff's daughter and son-in-law.

50. It is also contended that during the Plaintiff's statement recorded under Order X of the Code of Civil Procedure on 24.03.2022,
she admitted to having been dispossessed from the suit property in the year 2018, which is prior to the filing of the present suit.

The Plaintiff also stated that she has since been residing with her younger daughter and has not been permitted by the Defendant to re-enter or reside in the suit Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/
9 property.
51.

To support its claim, the Defendant has place on record copy of electricity bills (Ex.DW1/1 to DW1/2), copy of passport (Ex.DW1/3),
and copy of voter ID (Ex.DW1/4) showing his long-term residence at the suit property.
Although the Defendant also failed to produce registered documents of title, he claims the original documents were misplaced while shifting, and that an NCR was lodged with the police.
However, the NCR was also not placed on record.
52. It is correct position of law that a suit for permanent injunction is meant to protect lawful settled possession.
A party who is not in possession or has no enforceable legal right cannot seek an injunction.
Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 14 of 21  53.

Moving further, in Sudhakar Reddy Vs. Lakshmamma (2014 (4) ALT 647) it was held that "in a suit for perpetual injunction, the key consideration is who is in possession of the suit property as of the date of filing the suit.
The court may examine the title of the parties if circumstances so warrant."

54. Similarly, in Balkrishna Dattatreya Galande Vs Balkrishna Rambharose Gupta (2019 Law Suit (SC) 140) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in this case held that "in a suit under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a permanent injunction can only be granted to a person who is in actual possession of the property.

entities.text: Balkrishna Dattatreya Galande Vs Balkrishna Rambharose Gupta (2019 Law Suit (SC) 140)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The plaintiff must prove actual possession to secure a permanent injunction."
55.

Additionally, it is well-established in law, as stated in Maria Margarida Sequeria Fernandes and Ors. vs. Erasmo Jack de Sequeria (Dead) through L. Rs. (21.03.2012 - SC): MANU/SC/0225/2012, that "Possession is important when there are no title documents, but once title documents are presented, the title must be prioritized over possession."
Possession cannot be considered in a vacuum.
56.

sentences.text:
Upon perusal of evidence presented by the Plaintiff, it is evident that the core of the Plaintiff's case rests upon documents which include a registered General Power of Attorney (GPA), registered Will,
Affidavit, Agreement to Sell, Receipt and Possession Letter, which are unregistered.

57. However, as per Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act,
1882, read with Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908,
documents such as General Power of Attorney (GPA), Agreement to Sell,
Affidavit, Receipt, Possession Letter --even if registered--do not confer ownership rights in respect of immovable property.

58. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act clearly stipulates that the transfer of ownership in the case of immovable property valued at more than Rs. 100 can only be done through a registered sale deed.
Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 15 of 21

Therefore, in the present case, where the suit property is of value exceeding Rs. 100, no right, title, or interest can be claimed or created through any unregistered document or merely through a registered GPA.

Such documents, whether registered or unregistered, do not have the legal effect of conveying ownership or title, and as such, do not establish any Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/
10 lawful right over the suit property.

At best, on the basis of the registered agreement to sell, he could have claimed relief of specific performance in appropriate proceedings".

60. Additionally, the Plaintiff failed to prove the Will by not producing the death certificate of the testator or examining attesting witnesses, as required under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act,
1872.
There is also no registered sale deed, gift deed, or other valid document to support the Plaintiff's ownership claim.
No house tax receipts or other municipal records were filed.
Electricity bills were filed but not exhibited; hence, they cannot be read in evidence.
61. Moving further, the defence of section 53-A TPA,1882, is not available to Plaintiff.
As Section 53 -A can only be used as a shield, not a sword.
It does not confer ownership.
It protects the transferee against the transferor or anyone claiming through the transferor.
In this case, the Defendant is not the transferor, and hence, this doctrine cannot protect the Plaintiff.
62. The plaintiff still hasn't established her legal right of ownership of the suit property.

The documents she relies on registered GPA and notarised agreement to Sell, Affidavit, Possession Letter, Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 16 of 21 Receipt and registered Will are legally insufficient to transfer ownership or create any title.
As held in Shakeel Ahmed supra and Suraj Lamp & Industries supra, these documents don't convey ownership.
Without proving ownership, her claim that the defendant is a "licensee" becomes a hollow argument.
She cannot legally grant a license for a property she doesn't own.

63. Furthermore, a perusal of the Plaintiff's statement recorded under Order X of the Code of Civil Procedure clearly reveals that she admitted to having been dispossessed from the suit property by the Defendant as far back as the year 2018.
This admission unequivocally demonstrates that the Plaintiff was not in possession of the suit property at the time of filing the present suit.

Moreover,
the Plaintiff has not placed on record any cogent evidence to show that she took appropriate legal steps for the restoration or recovery of possession after such dispossession.
64. In contrast, the Defendant has demonstrated long-standing possession, supported by official documents, even though he also lacks registered ownership documents.
In cases where both parties lack formal title, continuous settled possession may tilt the balance in favour of the Defendant.
65. In such circumstances, the proper legal remedy available to the Plaintiff would have been to file a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession, and not merely a suit for injunction.
As held in Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594, where the title is in dispute and the Plaintiff is not in possession, a bare suit for injunction is not maintainable.

68. In light of the above findings and settled legal principles, the Plaintiff is not entitled to a decree of permanent or mandatory injunction.
Accordingly, this issue is decided against the Plaintiff.
Whether the plaintiff has not filed the appropriate court fees?
The burden to prove this issue lies upon the Defendant.
The Defendant has objected that the Plaintiff has not paid the correct court fees.
However, no evidence has been led to support this plea.
The Defendant has not filed any application under the Court Fees Act, nor provided the market value or circle rate of the property.
In absence of any evidence from the Defendant to support this contention.
Hence, this objection is not maintainable.
Accordingly, this issue is decided against the Defendant.
Whether the present suit of the plaintiff is not maintainable without claiming consequential relief?
The burden to prove this issue lies upon the Defendant.

The present suit has been filed by the Plaintiff seeking permanent and mandatory injunction against the Defendant, claiming herself to be the absolute owner of the suit property and alleging that Defendant was permitted to reside in the premises as a licensee.

The Plaintiff alleges that the Defendant and his family later dispossessed her,
and she now seeks Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 18 of 21 injunctive relief restraining them from interfering in the property and further directing them to vacate the premises.

71. However, as noted earlier (Issue No.1) that the ownership of the Plaintiff is under cloud and the Plaintiff, during her Order 10 CPC statement dated 05.05.2022, admitted that she was dispossessed in 2018, i.e., prior to the filing of the present suit, and that she has since been residing with her daughter.
Therefore, as of the date of institution of the suit, the Plaintiff was not in possession of the suit property.

72. It is a well-settled position of law that a bare suit for injunction is not maintainable when the title of Plaintiff is under cloud and Plaintiff is not in possession over the suit property at the time of filing the present suit.

In such circumstances, the Plaintiff must first seek a relief for declaration of title and recovery of possession, as these are consequential reliefs necessary for deciding the question of injunctive relief.

A suit for bare injunction would not be maintainable in such a case."

74. Since the Plaintiff was admittedly not in possession on the date of filing and her title is seriously disputed, a suit seeking only an injunction, without the necessary consequential reliefs of declaration of title and possession, is legally untenable.

Further, under Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, injunction shall not be granted when an efficacious remedy is available to the Plaintiff.
In this case, an appropriate remedy would have been a suit for declaration of ownership and recovery of possession, which the Plaintiff failed to pursue.

76. In view of the above analysis, it is held that the present suit, being one for mere injunction without seeking consequential reliefs, is not maintainable in law, particularly in light of the Plaintiff's admitted dispossession and disputed title.
Accordingly, this issue is decided in the favour of defendant.

In view of the findings returned on the issues above, particularly Issue Nos. 1 and 3, this Court is of the considered opinion that the Plaintiff has failed to establish lawful ownership or possession of the suit property as on the date of filing the present suit.

78. Further, in light of the serious and unresolved dispute regarding title, coupled with the Plaintiff's admitted lack of possession, the present suit for injunction simpliciter, without seeking declaration of title or recovery of possession, is not maintainable in law.
79. The Plaintiff has also failed to pursue the efficacious alternative remedies available to her under the law, as contemplated under Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Accordingly, the suit filed by the Plaintiff is hereby dismissed.
